title: Moving From Side Hustle to Business
summary: Side hustle → Steady growth → A real business
subtitle: Make the jump from side income to a business you can stand behind.

blocks.text: A side hustle becomes a business when it earns steadily, serves real customers and starts to need real structure. That moment can feel exciting and a little terrifying, like being handed the keys to a bus. This lesson puts the legal and tax steps in a sensible order, so growing up does not mean growing scared.
Take each step in order, and the jump feels like a staircase instead of a cliff.
blocks.detail: A clear order of small legal and money decisions lets you grow with confidence, and keeps your savings and your sleep safe.
blocks.extra: Section 03 compares the main business structures side by side.

blocks.text: To the CRA, you are already a business, even if your income is small. Self-employed income goes on Form T2125 with your personal return, whether you earn $500 or $50,000. What turns a hustle into a business is mostly how seriously you run it.

A good sign you are ready to grow is repeat demand: customers keep coming back or sending friends. Another sign is that the work is eating into your sleep. A third is that you keep turning down jobs you would love to take.
Growing does not mean quitting your day job tomorrow. Many owners spend a year or two building steady income on the side while they put the right structure in place.

The structure you pick decides who is responsible for the business’s debts, how its income is taxed and how much paperwork you handle. The two most common choices for a beginner are a sole proprietorship and a corporation.

items.title: Sole proprietorship
list: Legal identity: You and the business are the same person
Responsibility for debts: Business debts and claims can reach your personal assets
Tax filing: Business income goes on your T1 return with Form T2125
Losses: You report the loss on your own return

items.title: Corporation
list: Legal identity: A separate legal entity
Responsibility for debts: Shareholders are generally not responsible for its debts, though lenders may ask for a personal guarantee
Tax filing: The corporation files its own T2 return within six months of its year-end
Losses: Shareholders cannot claim the corporation’s losses
Setup effort: More paperwork, ongoing filings, and professional fees

blocks.text: Neither structure wins every time. A corporation can offer protection and tax planning choices, but it also brings extra costs and rules. Talk to an accountant and a lawyer about your own numbers before you decide. This lesson explains the choices. It does not pick one for you.

items.title: “Incorporating means I never have to worry about debts or lawsuits.”
items.text: A lender may ask you to personally guarantee a loan. Directors can also be personally liable if the company fails to send in certain amounts it owes, such as payroll deductions. Insurance and good contracts still matter.

blocks.text: Register and get your numbers

Most businesses must register with the province or territory where they operate, though a sole proprietor using their own name may not need to. In British Columbia, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Saskatchewan, you get a federal business number when you register with the province. Elsewhere, you apply to the CRA for one.

A business number is a nine-digit ID. You link tax accounts to it, such as a GST/HST account, when you need them. Check which permits and licences your city, province and industry require. The free BizPaL tool can list them for you.

Regulated trades need more than a business number. Electricians, plumbers, gas fitters and some other trades need a licence and often a permit for each job before they work for the public. In B.C., for example, Technical Safety BC requires a licence to be hired for electrical work and a permit for every EV charger install.
Keep your business money separate. A separate bank account makes your records cleaner, your return simpler and your story easier to tell if the CRA, a lender or a landlord ever asks.
Plan for the taxes that come with growth

As your profit grows, you may have to pay income tax in instalments during the year instead of one lump sum when you file. For 2026, the CRA says you must pay instalments if your net tax owing is more than $3,000 ($1,800 in Quebec) and it was also above that in 2025 or 2024. Your instalments also cover the CPP you owe on your own earnings.

Self-employed people pay both halves of CPP. Once your net self-employment income passes $3,500 in a year, you pay Canada Pension Plan contributions on it, covering both the worker and employer shares. Quebec residents pay into the Quebec Pension Plan instead.
Before you cut your hours

items.title: A CASH CUSHION
items.text: Save three to six months of household costs before you leave a steady paycheque. Self-employed income comes in waves.

items.title: HEALTH AND DENTAL
items.text: Your job’s benefits plan ends when the job does. Price a personal health and dental plan and add it to your costs.

items.title: EI SPECIAL BENEFITS
items.text: Self-employed people can sign up for EI special benefits, such as sickness and parental leave. You pay premiums, and you must wait 12 months after signing up before you can claim.

items.title: NO MORE PAYROLL TAX
items.text: No one takes tax off your business income. Move a share of every payment into a tax account, and plan for instalments.

blocks.text: The Voltage Tester
paragraphs: Mehdi Karimi worked as an electrician in Surrey. In the evenings he installed electric-vehicle chargers for neighbours. His goal was to cut his day job to four days a week, so he could spend the fifth day on his own customers. A yellow voltage tester hung from his belt.

By spring he had eleven repeat clients. Then a property manager asked if he had liability insurance, a contractor licence and a business number. The company needed all three before it could give him a bigger contract. Mehdi had none of them.

That night he searched online and found a forum full of advice. A dozen people said the same thing: “Incorporate right now.” Mehdi felt a rush of panic. His finger hovered over a button that offered to set up a company for a flat fee.

He stopped and made a different choice. He would not rush into a company because strangers told him to. He booked an hour with an accountant and brought his numbers. His profit was about $22,000 a year. For now, they agreed, a sole proprietorship with good insurance made more sense. They set a review date and wrote down the profit level that would make him think again.

Mehdi registered his business name and got his business number. He applied to Technical Safety BC for his contractor licence and started pulling a permit for every install. He bought liability insurance and opened a business bank account. Then he sent the property manager his papers.

The manager hired him, and the questions helped. She liked how well he had answered them. By autumn Mehdi had moved to a four-day job. By the next review his profit had passed the level he wrote down, and he went back to the accountant with a smile. The yellow voltage tester still hangs from his belt.

blocks.text: Slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.
blocks.detail: A planned structure, the right paperwork and an honest review date protect your income and make you look as professional as you are.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a step-by-step plan for your own move.

items.title: Check your readiness.
items.text: Look for repeat customers, steady income and more demand than free time.

items.title: Choose a structure with advice.
items.text: Compare the options with an accountant and a lawyer who can see your real numbers.

items.title: Register and get your numbers.
items.text: Register with your province, get a business number, add tax accounts as you need them, and get any licence your trade requires.

items.title: Protect the business.
items.text: Open a business bank account, and ask an insurance broker about liability coverage for your type of work.

items.title: Plan for tax.
items.text: Set money aside for income tax, CPP and GST/HST, and check whether you must pay instalments.

items.title: Set a review date.
items.text: Decide ahead of time what profit or risk would make you look at your structure again.

blocks.text: Notes by province, and for your taxes

items.title: Registration
items.text: Rules differ by province. Newfoundland and Labrador has no provincial registration for sole proprietorships, while most other provinces require it in many cases.

items.title: Quebec
items.text: Quebec uses the Quebec Pension Plan and has its own business registry, the Registraire des entreprises, so check its rules.

items.title: GST/HST
items.text: You must register once your taxable sales pass $30,000 over four calendar quarters, or in a single quarter.

items.title: “I have to quit my job before I can call myself a business.”
items.text: You can run a real business on the side, with a business number, proper records and registered accounts. Many people do that for years.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Write down your review trigger today, such as a profit amount or a number of clients. It gives you a calm, planned reason to look at your structure again, instead of a stressful one.
Quick Check

items.title: Where do you report self-employed income as a sole proprietor?
items.detail: On your T1 return, using Form T2125.

items.title: In a corporation, can shareholders claim the corporation’s losses?
items.text: The corporation’s losses stay with the corporation.

items.title: When must you pay income tax by instalments?
items.detail: When your net tax owing is above the CRA’s threshold in the current year and in one of the two years before.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Who is responsible for a sole proprietorship’s debts? A. The business alone · B. You personally · C. The CRA
items.text: A sole proprietorship has no separate legal identity, so business debts can reach your personal assets.

items.title: Which form reports a sole proprietor’s business income? A. Form T2125 · B. Form T137 · C. Form T2
items.text: Form T2125 is attached to your personal T1 return. A T2 return is the corporation’s.

items.title: Why set a review date for your business structure? A. So you can change structure when your numbers change · B. Because the CRA requires it · C. So you never have to think about it again
items.text: Your best structure can change as your profit and risk change.

items.title: In one sentence, describe the first step you will take toward becoming a business.
items.text: I will open a business bank account and book an hour with an accountant next month.

blocks.text: Grow in order: check readiness, choose a structure with advice, register, protect the business, plan for tax, and set a review date.

items.title: Corporation
items.text: A business that is a legal person, separate from its owners.

items.title: Sole proprietorship
items.text: A business owned by one person that is not incorporated.

items.title: Program account
items.text: A CRA account for one tax, such as GST/HST.

items.title: Business number
items.text: A nine-digit number the CRA uses to identify your business.

items.title: Shareholder
items.text: An owner of a corporation who holds shares in it.

items.title: Instalments
items.text: Tax payments you make during the year instead of all at once when you file.
